explain: A fund with a large share portfolio buys index puts so a market fall is offset by the put's gain. It accepts a small certain cost (the premium) for protection. Domestic mutual funds and insurers are the main example. A put held this way says nothing about where the fund thinks the market goes.

A trader buys puts, or sells futures, because they expect a fall. Foreign institutions that hold large net short index futures together with net long puts are doing this or hedging a long cash book; their futures and options positions together tell which.

Proprietary desks and the retail crowd often sell puts and calls to collect time decay. Most of the time it works; a fast move against the seller is what costs. Put selling is the opposite view to put buying and is common, not rare.

Large trading firms quote options both ways and hedge each trade with futures or shares. Their put buying is usually one leg of a hedged position (a spread against futures, a volatility trade, a basket against the index), so it is not a one-way market view.

Positions around expiry days and big events (budget, results, rate decisions) can be large and short-lived: puts are bought for a jump in volatility, then sold. SEBI has been tightening the rules for expiry-day trading because the size of some of these positions can move the index itself.
summary: Foreign institutions are net short 70,670 index futures with net long puts and net short calls, which together behave like a short index position. That is a bearish or hedged stance, and futures were net short in every one of the last 6 sessions.
Domestic institutions hold +114,129 net puts and +22,914 futures: the puts are insurance on the funds' share portfolios, so they are not a forecast of a fall.
Proprietary desks and market makers are close to flat (-11,915 futures, -15,838 puts, +24,273 calls). Their put buying is mostly one leg of a hedged trade.
Retail and other clients are the largest put sellers (-472,490 net puts): the crowd is betting the market will not fall, which is why a sharp fall hurts them most.
